title: Separation of powers
body: Many constitutions split government into three branches: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them. The idea, linked to the French thinker Montesquieu, is that each branch checks the others.

title: Where 'democracy' comes from
body: The word democracy comes from the Greek 'demos' (people) and 'kratos' (power or rule): rule by the people. Ancient Athens practised an early direct form of it in the 5th century BCE.

title: Parliamentary systems
body: In a parliamentary system the head of government (usually a prime minister) comes from and depends on the support of parliament. If parliament loses confidence in the government, it can be removed. Examples include the UK, India and Japan.

title: Presidential systems
body: In a presidential system the president is both head of state and head of government, is elected separately from the legislature, and serves a fixed term. Examples include the United States, Brazil and Kenya.

title: What is federalism?
body: In a federal system, power is shared between a national government and regional governments such as states or provinces, each with its own powers set by the constitution. Examples: the United States, Nigeria, India and Germany.

title: What is a unitary state?
body: In a unitary state the central government holds most power. Local governments exist, but their powers are given, and can be changed, by the centre. France and Japan are examples.

title: What a constitution does
body: A constitution is the supreme law of a country. It sets out how government is organised, what powers each part has, and often the rights of citizens. Other laws must not contradict it.

title: Magna Carta, 1215
body: In 1215 King John of England agreed to Magna Carta, a charter limiting royal power. Its principle that even the ruler is subject to the law influenced later constitutions around the world.

title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
body: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948. It sets out 30 articles of basic rights. 10 December is now Human Rights Day.
source_name: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

title: First past the post
body: Under 'first past the post', each area elects one representative: whoever gets the most votes wins, even without a majority. It is simple, but a party's share of seats can differ a lot from its share of votes.

title: Proportional representation
body: In proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in line with their share of the vote. 30% of votes gives about 30% of seats. It often leads to coalition governments. South Africa and the Netherlands use forms of it.

title: What is a referendum?
body: A referendum is a direct vote in which all voters decide on a single question, such as a new constitution or leaving an organisation, instead of leaving the decision to elected representatives.

title: Constitutional monarchy
body: In a constitutional monarchy, a king or queen is head of state but their powers are limited by a constitution, and elected politicians run the government. Examples: the UK, Japan and Lesotho. In an absolute monarchy, the monarch holds full power.

title: Two chambers
body: A bicameral legislature has two chambers, such as a lower house and an upper house or senate. Laws usually need approval from both. A unicameral legislature has only one chamber.

title: The rule of law
body: The rule of law means everyone, including government leaders, is subject to laws that are public, applied equally and decided by independent courts, rather than to the arbitrary will of those in power.

title: South Africa's 1994 election
body: South Africa's first election in which all races could vote was held in April 1994. Nelson Mandela became the country's first democratically elected president in May 1994.

title: The Berlin Wall falls
body: The Berlin Wall, which divided East and West Berlin from 1961, was opened on 9 November 1989. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.

title: Women's right to vote
body: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all women the right to vote in national elections.
source_name: Wikipedia: Women's suffrage in New Zealand

title: What is impeachment?
body: Impeachment is a process in which a legislature formally charges a senior official, such as a president, with serious misconduct. Depending on the country, a conviction can lead to removal from office.

title: Coalition governments
body: When no single party wins a majority, two or more parties may agree to govern together as a coalition, sharing ministries and agreeing a common programme.

title: Judicial review
body: Judicial review is the power of courts to check whether laws or government actions follow the constitution, and to strike them down if they do not.

title: Head of state vs head of government
body: The head of state represents the country, often in a ceremonial role. The head of government runs the government day to day. In some countries one person does both; in others, like Germany, they are separate.

title: Why 'left' and 'right'?
body: The terms left and right in politics come from the French Revolution. In the National Assembly of 1789, supporters of the king sat on the right of the president and supporters of revolution on the left.

title: Term limits
body: A term limit restricts how many times, or how long, a person can hold an office. Many presidential systems limit presidents to two terms. Supporters see them as a check on power; critics say voters should decide.

title: Ghana's independence, 1957
body: Ghana, formerly the Gold Coast, gained independence from Britain on 6 March 1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah. It was among the first colonies in sub-Saharan Africa to become independent.

title: The role of the opposition
body: Parties not in government form the opposition. They question and scrutinise the government, propose alternative policies and offer voters a choice at the next election.

title: Politics word: sovereignty
body: Meaning: supreme authority of a state to govern itself without outside interference.
example_sentence: The treaty respects each country's sovereignty over its own borders.

title: Politics word: manifesto
body: Meaning: a public statement of a party's policies and aims, usually published before an election.
example_sentence: The party's manifesto promised free school meals.

title: Politics word: constituency
body: Meaning: an area whose voters elect a representative, and also the voters themselves.
example_sentence: She held regular meetings with people in her constituency.

title: Politics word: veto
body: Meaning: the power to reject a decision or law. From Latin for 'I forbid'.
example_sentence: The president used a veto to block the bill.

title: Politics word: incumbent
body: Meaning: the person who currently holds an office.
example_sentence: The incumbent mayor is running for a second term.

title: Politics word: electorate
body: Meaning: all the people entitled to vote in an election.
example_sentence: Young people make up a growing share of the electorate.

title: Where prime ministers come from
body: Systems of government.
statement: In a parliamentary system, the head of government usually comes from the legislature
explanation: The prime minister is usually a member of parliament and needs its support to stay in office.

title: Who makes laws?
body: Branches of government.
statement: The judiciary's main role is to make laws
explanation: The legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out and the judiciary interprets and applies them.

title: Magna Carta date
body: History check.
explanation: King John agreed to Magna Carta in 1215, six centuries earlier.

title: Direct democracy
body: Voting check.
statement: A referendum lets citizens vote directly on a specific question
explanation: In a referendum voters decide one question themselves instead of leaving it to representatives.

title: Human rights declaration
body: History check.
statement: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948
explanation: The UN General Assembly adopted it on 10 December 1948 in Paris.
source_name: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

title: Federal power
body: Systems of government.
statement: In a federal system, all power belongs to the central government
explanation: Federal systems share power between national and regional governments. Central control describes a unitary state.

title: Mandela's presidency
body: History check.
statement: Nelson Mandela became president of South Africa in 1994
explanation: He was inaugurated in May 1994 after the country's first fully democratic election.

title: The Berlin Wall
body: History check.
explanation: The wall was opened on 9 November 1989. German reunification followed in 1990.

title: Counting chambers
body: Parliament check.
explanation: 'Bi' means two. A bicameral parliament has two houses, such as an assembly and a senate.
